# Was the Microsoft 365 outage a cyberattack?

**Debunked.** All the public evidence says no. Microsoft says it was a technical failure, and the US government said on Nov 18 that the outage was not a cyberattack. Microsoft's final report, dated Nov 20, also says it was not a cyberattack.

Incident: Microsoft 365 outage, Nov 12-13, 2026. Also reported as the Microsoft outage. First published Nov 18, 2026; last updated Nov 22, 2026, 1:50 AM ET.

Picture: Building 92 at Microsoft's headquarters in Redmond, Washington, in May 2016. Image: Coolcaesar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Building92microsoft.jpg).

> **Not verified: initial investigation only.** Nothing on this page is absolutely confirmed. It is an early look based only on publicly available sources, and it should not be treated as verified fact. Even items labeled "Confirmed" only mean a public source reports them. Made for entertainment using AI. Not endorsed by Microsoft, any government agency, news outlet, company, or anyone else named.

This is the current answer, not a final verdict.

## The latest

Nov 22, 2026, 1:50 AM ET: **The Guardian, an established outlet, now describes the cause given in Microsoft's final report.** The Guardian published an explainer on Nov 22 about the recent run of outages. It says a July upgrade left a software bug in place that lay dormant for months until a string of coincidences triggered it and overwhelmed Microsoft's servers, which matches Microsoft's final report. Added as a further source for c020 (the final report's account of the cause). No label changed and the main answer is unchanged.

## At a glance

- Status: monitoring
- Size: Large. Exchange Online email is a service many organizations and governments rely on every day. Microsoft says most users were affected for about 24 hours, and problems were reported in at least 70 countries. This is actual impact, not potential.
- Who is affected: Most Microsoft 365 business, school and government users who rely on Exchange Online or Outlook for email. This was a service outage, not a breach. Be wary of emails about the outage that ask you to click to restore held messages.

| Value | What | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| ~24 hours | Length of the outage | 11:20 AM ET Nov 12 to 11:10 AM ET Nov 13 |
| 70+ | Countries reporting problems | BBC News |
| 80%+ | Gateway servers unresponsive at worst | Microsoft's preliminary report |
| ~14% | Gateway capacity already out of service | Microsoft's preliminary report |
| Nov 20 | Final report released | Microsoft, per GeekWire |

### Known so far

- Exchange Online and Outlook were down for most users from 11:20 AM ET Nov 12 to 11:10 AM ET Nov 13, per Microsoft's report.
- Most users could not reach their mailboxes, and parts of Teams, Copilot, SharePoint and OneDrive were also affected.
- Microsoft's preliminary report blames a latent defect from a July update, set off by extra traffic and reduced capacity. This is Microsoft's own finding.
- Microsoft's final report, dated Nov 20, gives the same cause and says the outage was confirmed not to be a cyberattack. This is Microsoft's own finding.

### Not known yet

- Why the Teams routing issue in Microsoft's US East region happened, and what the July update was meant to fix. The final report does not say.
- Whether any independent body will publish its own finding on the cause. None has; the answer that it was not a cyberattack rests on Microsoft's report and the US government's statement.
- Exactly how many users and organizations were affected.
- When Microsoft's promised fixes, such as smaller fault zones and separate gateway pools for each workload, will be in place. Its final report dates several for early 2027.
- Whether the phishing campaign stole any credentials. Microsoft says this has not been confirmed.

## Official statements

> We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. [...] This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.
>
> — Microsoft, on its official X account, Nov 13

> First, a latent defect caused Windows servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions. [...] This defect was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers; neither the underlying defect nor the fix applies to broader Windows deployments.
>
> — Microsoft Preliminary Post Incident Report, Nov 15 (third-party copy)

> This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity. This change was not caused by AI tooling.
>
> — Microsoft Post Incident Report, Nov 20 (third-party copy)

> This is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state.
>
> — Director of National Intelligence, quoted by the White House, Nov 18

## What we checked and did not find

- Microsoft's own copy of the preliminary post-incident report. Not checked: it needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login. We cite a third-party copy, labeled as such.
- Microsoft's own copy of the final post-incident report, dated Nov 20. Not checked: it needs a Microsoft 365 admin-center login. We cite a third-party copy, labeled as such.
- Coverage of the final report by established news outlets. Not found as of 8:50 AM ET on Nov 21.
- Any credible claim of a hack, breach or attacker behind the outage. Not found.
- A major Azure outage on Nov 18, 2026. Not found.
- AP's article on the recovery. Not checked: access blocked.
